Question: What are the properties of noble gases? Are all metals in group one noble gases or are there some exceptions to this rule? If so, what are they and why aren't they considered as such?
Answer: There are two different numbering systems for the periodic table. The noble gasses are in group VIIIA or Group 18, depending which system you use. None of them are metals by the conventional definition of metals, but astronomers would call all of the noble gasses metals except for helium. According to astronomers all elements except hydrogen and helium are “metals”, All of the noble gasses are monatomic gasses at room temperature with the possible exception of element 118 Oganesson. Oganesson is a synthetic element and only six atoms have ever been made, so determination of physical properties has been difficult. The heavier noble gasses have higher boiling points. Thus the boiling point of the lightest, helium, is -268.9 °C whereas the boiling point of the heaviest naturally occurring noble gas, radon, is -61.7 °C. At one time it was thought that noble gasses cannot form chemical compounds because their outer electron shells are filled. However, in 1962 Xenon was combines with fluorine to make Xenon Fluoride XeF4. A few other compounds have since been discovered. Group 1 of the periodic table contains the highly reactive alkali metals. All of group 1 are metals even by conventional definitions except hydrogen.

Question: What is the most common metal in the Earth’s crust?
Answer: The most common metal in the Earth’s crust is aluminum, as indicated in the following table. The reason for aluminum being the most common metal is that feldspar is the most common mineral in the Earth’s crust, accounting for about 60% of the Earth’s crust by mass. Feldspars are a whole family of minerals with variable and complex compositions - but they all contain aluminum. For example the formula for Albite is NaAlSi3O8, whereas the chemical formula for Anorthite is CaAl2Si2O8 and Orthoclase is KAlSi3O8. All three minerals are in the feldspar family.

Question: Why did British Prime Minister Winston Churchill reportedly have such a low opinion of General Montgomery?
Answer: I don’t know where you get that idea from. It’s true that Montgomery was not Churchill’s first choice for commander of the eighth army. Churchill preferred William Gott - but Gott was killed in an air crash and Montgomery got the job. However once Churchill saw Montgomery could win battles he was a strong supporter. Churchill could still have a sharp tongue - he said of Montgomery “In defeat, unbeatable: in victory, unbearable.” Montgomery’s first great victory was at Alamein. To maintain his position with the Americans, Churchill desperatly needed a British victory in North Africa before the joint Torch landings. Montgomery gave it to him. Churchill wrote “Before Alamein we never had a victory. After Alamein we never had a defeat.” Churchill visited Montgomery on the battlefield, most notably during the crossing of the Rhine. Here are the two of them together on that occasion. In September 1944, Churchill had Montgomery promoted to Field Marshall - a five star general compared to Eisenhower’s four stars. After the war, Montgomery was invited to Churchill’s home at Cherwell several times, so I can’t see how he was not well respected by Churchill.

Question: What is the reason for the absence of liquid oxygen on Earth's surface?
Answer: There is plenty of liquid oxygen on the Earth’s surface. For example, NASA has a big storage tank of it at the Kennedy Space Centre. Liquefaction of air is the most common way of separating oxygen from air for industrial or recreational purposes, so it is quite common. Of course, the fact that it boils at minus 183 degrees Celsius means that it has to be kept in special tanks. This video explains the liquefaction process.

Question: How accurate is carbon dating, and what use can you make with it?
Answer: Carbon dating in theory can be highly accurate, but it needs meticulous attention to detail and a deep understanding of the process to achieve accuracy. Carbon dating relies on measuring the ratio of carbon 14 to carbon 12 in a sample. Carbon has two stable isotopes - carbon 12 and carbon 13. Carbon 14 is an unstable isotope with a half life of 5,730 years. On Earth 99% of carbon is Carbon 12, 1% is Carbon 13 and 1.5 atoms in a quadrillion are Carbon 14. Cosmic rays striking the atmosphere produce neutrons. The neutrons react with Nitrogen 14 to produce carbon 14 plus a proton according to the formula: The carbon 14 oxidises to carbon dioxide. Plants absorb carbon dioxide and through photosynthesis convert it to solid plant material. The carbon 14 is absorbed along with the carbon 12 and carbon 13. While the plant is alive, the ratio of carbon 14 to carbon 12 is the same as in the atmosphere. After the plant dies, the carbon 14 decays back to nitrogen 14. After 5,730 years, half of the carbon 14 has gone. By measuring the ratio of carbon 14 to carbon 12 and carbon 13, it is possible to calculate the time that has elapsed since the plant material was created. Assumptions that are made to arrive at a result are: It is known that the ratio of carbon 14 has not been constant. It varies with cosmic ray intensity. By comparing with other dating methods - such as tree rings, it has been possible to develop a correction for varying carbon 14 concentrations - as in the graph below Thus if the the uncorrected age is calculated to be 30,000 years, the real age is 34,000 years. Mass spectrometers are amazingly sensitive and accurate devices. Their accuracy must be maintained by regular use of standard samples of known age. Sample preparation is complex and must be done meticulously. Contamination with modern carbon is a very real issue with older samples. A 38,000 year old sample contains only 1% of the original carbon 14. A small amount of modern carbon contamination will give a large error. Contamination can occur at any stage of the process from collection to sample preparation. Things like microbial growth on the sample or inclusion of modern air must be guarded against. Any dates older than 40,000 years must be considered suspect. Dates younger than this determined by reputable laboratories can be considered highly accurate. It must be remembered that the date determined is the date on which the plant material was formed. Thus in New Mexico we used carbon dating to determine the age of wood used in habitations. But, in the New Mexico desert, wood can survive undecomposed for hundreds of years. The date determined is the date of the wood. It could have been used to build a hut many years later. Also in a tree the center of the tree will have an older date than the outside. Other organic material can also used - for example animal remains. The date will reflect the age of the food eaten. Shells cannot be used. This is because the calcium carbonate in shells likely was dissolved in water and did not represent the carbon 14 in the atmosphere at the time the shell was formed. In summary, carbon dating can be used to determine the date of organic material up to about 40,000 years old. The organic material could for example be wooden artefacts. If determined by a reputable laboratory after careful sample collection and treatment, the dates are very accurate.
